title: Durability: the fourth dimension
goal: Explain what durability (physiological resilience) is, its two parts (onset and magnitude), and why fresh-test values of VO2max, threshold and economy mislead late in long events.

steps.title: Three numbers from a fresh test

claims.text: Start-line VO2max, fractional utilisation and economy predict endurance performance, but they are not static and deteriorate during fatiguing endurance exercise.

evidence.quote: while 'start line' values of these variables are collectively useful in predicting performance in endurance events such as the marathon, it is not widely appreciated that these variables are not static but are prone to significant deterioration as fatiguing endurance exercise proceeds.
the attributes measured during routine physiological-profiling assessments are not static, but change over time during prolonged exercise.

steps.title: Durability: onset and magnitude
steps.text:
*Fatigue in long efforts* introduced [durability](g:durability). Maunder and colleagues define it as **the time of onset and the magnitude of deterioration** in the physiological profile during prolonged exercise [[c:dc-maunder-def]]. Two numbers, then:

- **onset**: how long before a threshold, efficiency or power starts to slip;
- **magnitude**: how far it has slipped by a given point.

A later review puts it as resilience to the decline of physiological variables and performance during or after prolonged exercise [[c:dc-hunter-def]]. Andrew Jones calls the same idea [physiological resilience](g:physiological-resilience).

Durability is not the same as 'being fit'. Two athletes with equal fresh numbers can drift at different times and by different amounts.

claims.text: Durability is the time of onset and magnitude of deterioration in physiological-profiling characteristics over time during prolonged exercise.

evidence.quote: quantify the 'durability' of individual athletes, here defined as the time of onset and magnitude of deterioration in physiological-profiling characteristics over time during prolonged exercise.

claims.text: Durability has been defined as resilience to the deterioration of physiological variables and performance during or following prolonged exercise.

evidence.quote: Durability has been defined as the resilience to the deterioration of physiological variables and performance during or following prolonged exercise.

steps.title: Same fresh numbers, different hour four
steps.text:
How much do the numbers drift? [Critical power](g:critical-power) (CP) falls by about **10%** on average after 2 h of [heavy-intensity](g:heavy-domain) cycling. The spread between people is wide: from **under 1% to about 32%** [[c:dc-cp-spread]].

That spread shows up in racing. In 112 male professionals, WorldTour and the level below (ProTeam) had no consistent difference in fresh best powers. After a lot of work already done, the WorldTour riders held clearly higher power, especially for efforts of 5 min and longer [[c:dc-wt-pt]].

So a fresh test can rank two riders as equal while the race, decided in the last hour, does not.

claims.text: Critical power may fall by about 10% on average after 2 h of heavy-intensity cycling, with individual changes from under 1% to about 32%.

evidence.quote: For example, the 'critical power' (CP), which is a composite of the highest achievable steady-state oxidative metabolic rate and efficiency (O2 cost per watt), may fall by an average of 10% following 2 h of heavy intensity cycle exercise.
Even more striking is that the extent of this deterioration displays appreciable inter-individual variability, with changes in CP ranging from <1% to ∼32%.

claims.text: WorldTour and ProTeam cyclists did not differ consistently in fresh mean maximal power, but WorldTour riders were higher after accumulated work, especially for efforts of 5 min or longer.

evidence.quote: No consistent differences were found between WT and PT cyclists in MMP values assessed in nonfatigue conditions (after 0 kJ·kg-1), but WT cyclists attained significantly higher MMP values with accumulating levels of fatigue, particularly for long-duration efforts (≥5 min).

steps.title: A fourth dimension?
steps.text:
Jones argues that resilience should be added to the three pillars as a **fourth dimension** of endurance performance. He also says plainly that why some people are more resilient is not yet known [[c:dc-fourth-dim]].

Is it really separate from the other three? The evidence is split. In 20 amateur road cyclists, the drop in 5 and 20 min power after 1,000 kJ of riding was not related to [VO2max](g:vo2max) or [FTP](g:ftp) per kg [[c:dc-independent]]. But in 10 young professionals, the riders with higher VO₂max, thresholds and efficiency kept more of their CP after hard intervals [[c:dc-predicted]].

Both studies are small, and both are snapshots ([cross-sectional](g:cross-sectional-study)): they show what goes together, not cause.

claims.text: Physiological resilience should be considered a fourth dimension in models of endurance performance; its mechanisms are not resolved.

evidence.quote: This article presents new information concerning the dynamic plasticity of the three 'traditional' physiological variables and argues that physiological resilience should be considered as an additional component, or fourth dimension, in models of endurance exercise performance.
The mechanistic basis for such differences in fatigue resistance or 'physiological resilience' are not resolved.

claims.text: In 20 amateur cyclists, 5 and 20 min power fell about 10% after 1,000 kJ, and durability was not correlated with VO2max or relative FTP.

evidence.quote: The performance significantly decreased with 10,1 ± 6,5% in the 20-minutes test and with 10,8 ± 7,8% in 5-minutes in fatigue state in compare with fresh state.
No significant correlations were found between better durability and VO2 max or relative FTP.

claims.text: In 10 professional cyclists, the share of CP kept after fatiguing intervals correlated with relative VO2max, ventilatory-threshold power and gross efficiency.

evidence.quote: Significant positive relationships were found between ∆CP and relative peak power output ( r = 0.891, P < 0.001), relative maximum oxygen uptake ( r = 0.835, P = 0.003)

debate.question: Is durability independent of VO2max, thresholds and economy?

sides.position: Yes, largely: athletes with similar fresh values differ a lot in how much they decline, and in amateurs the decline was unrelated to VO2max or FTP.
Partly not: in professional cyclists, higher fresh VO2max, thresholds and efficiency predicted a smaller fall in CP, so the fresh profile explains much of durability.

steps.title: What it changes in practice
steps.text:
If the numbers drift, fresh-test values mislead whenever they are used late in a long session: for setting intensity, tracking training load, judging adaptations and predicting performance [[c:dc-uses]].

Running gives the clearest picture. In 82,303 marathon runners, heart rate rose relative to pace as the race went on, first detected at about **25 km** on average. People differed a lot, and those who drifted least ran faster [[c:dc-marathon]].

For a triathlete, the same logic covers the whole race: the run of an Ironman starts after 180 km of cycling, so fresh run zones are optimistic from the first step.

claims.text: Unaccounted shifts in physiological attributes during prolonged exercise affect intensity regulation, measuring adaptation, training-load monitoring and performance prediction.

evidence.quote: If not accounted for, shifts in these physiological attributes during prolonged exercise have implications for the accuracy of their use in intensity regulation during prolonged training sessions or competitions, quantifying training adaptations, training-load programming and monitoring, and the prediction of exercise performance.

claims.text: In 82,303 marathon runners, the heart-rate-to-speed ratio drifted on average from about 25 km; the magnitude and onset varied widely and were associated with marathon performance.

evidence.quote: The overall internal-to-external workload decoupling experienced was 1.16 ± 0.22, first detected 25.2 ± 9.9 km into marathon running.
Durability characteristics, assessed as internal-to-external workload ratio, show considerable inter-individual variability, and both its magnitude and onset are associated with marathon performance.

points: The classic model rests on three fresh-test pillars: VO₂max, the share of it you can hold, and economy.
Those values aren't fixed: they worsen during prolonged exercise. Durability is when (onset) and how much (magnitude).
Critical power falls about 10% on average after 2 h of heavy cycling, from under 1% to about 32% between people.
Fatigued power, not fresh power, separated WorldTour from ProTeam riders; Jones proposes resilience as a fourth dimension.
Whether durability is independent of the three pillars is debated; the evidence is small and cross-sectional.
Fresh zones overestimate late-race capacity in a marathon, a long road race or an Ironman run.

variants.stem: Which three fresh-test variables make up the classic model of endurance performance?

options.text: VO₂max, the share of it you can hold, and economy
options.why: Right: the three pillars, all measured on rested athletes.

options.text: VO₂max, maximal heart rate and body mass
options.why: Maximal heart rate doesn't predict endurance performance; it varies with age and genes.

options.text: Sprint power, VO₂max and muscle glycogen
options.why: Sprint power and glycogen matter in some events but aren't the three pillars.

options.text: Lactate threshold, sweat rate and economy
options.why: Sweat rate isn't one of the pillars; VO₂max is missing.

variants.stem: Two marathoners have the same VO₂max, threshold pace and running economy, measured fresh. One finishes 6 minutes ahead. Best explanation?

options.text: Her economy and threshold held up better in the last part of the race
options.why: Right: start-line values are equal, but they drift during the race, and by different amounts.

options.text: The lab test must have been wrong for one of them
options.why: Possible, but the simpler reason is that the variables change during the race.

options.text: Fresh values fully predict the result, so it must be luck
options.why: Fresh values predict well on average, but they aren't static; a 6 min gap has a physiological cause.

options.text: She had a higher maximal heart rate
options.why: Maximal heart rate isn't a determinant of endurance performance.

variants.stem: Runner A's economy starts to worsen after 60 min and is 3% worse at 3 h. Runner B's holds until 2 h, then is 8% worse at 3 h. Which is correct?

options.text: A has the earlier onset; B has the larger magnitude by 3 h
options.why: Right: durability has two parts, onset and magnitude, and they need not go together.

options.text: A is less durable on both counts
options.why: A's onset is earlier, but by 3 h B has drifted more.

options.text: B is more durable on both counts
options.why: B's onset is later, but B's magnitude by 3 h is larger.

options.text: They can't be compared: durability needs a lab test
options.why: Economy measured during a long run is exactly how durability is tracked.

options.text: When and how much the physiological profile worsens during prolonged exercise
options.why: Right: onset and magnitude of the decline (Maunder's definition).

options.text: How high the physiological profile is when fresh
options.why: That's the fresh profile itself, not how it holds up.

options.text: How quickly an athlete recovers after a long race
options.why: Recovery is a separate topic; durability is about the decline during the effort.

options.text: How many years an athlete stays at the top level
options.why: That's career longevity, not physiological durability.

variants.stem: Two pro cyclists have the same fresh 20 min best. In a 5 h race the climb that decides it starts after 4 h. Which data would best tell you who is likely to climb faster?

options.text: Each rider's best 20 min power after a lot of work already done
options.why: Right: fresh values didn't separate WorldTour from ProTeam riders; fatigued values did.

options.text: Their fresh 20 min power, measured again
options.why: They're already equal on it, and fresh values didn't separate the levels.

options.text: Their fresh 10 s sprint power
options.why: A sprint value says little about a 20 min climb after 4 h.

options.text: Their resting heart rate
options.why: Resting heart rate doesn't predict late-race power.

variants.stem: After 2 h of heavy-intensity cycling, how much does critical power typically fall, and how much do people differ?

options.text: About 10% on average, from under 1% to about 32%
options.why: Right: a sizable average fall with a very wide spread.

options.text: About 1% on average, the same in everyone
options.why: CP isn't fixed: it falls about 10%, and people differ a lot.

options.text: About 30% on average, the same in everyone
options.why: About 30% is near the top of the range, not the average.

options.text: It doesn't fall: CP is a fixed property
options.why: Treating CP as fixed is exactly what durability research overturned.

variants.stem: One study finds durability unrelated to VO₂max in amateurs; another finds it strongly related to VO₂max in professionals. What is the fairest conclusion?

options.text: It's open: both are small cross-sectional studies in different groups
options.why: Right: n = 20 and n = 10, different protocols and levels; neither settles it.

options.text: Durability is fully independent of VO₂max
options.why: One small study in amateurs can't establish that, and the other study disagrees.

options.text: Durability is just VO₂max measured another way
options.why: One study of 10 riders can't prove that, and the amateur study found no link at all.

options.text: The professional study wins because pros matter more
options.why: Status of the athletes doesn't make a 10-rider study stronger evidence.

variants.stem: In 10 young pro cyclists, the share of CP kept after hard intervals correlated with VO₂max (r = 0.84). What most limits this finding?

options.text: Ten riders, one snapshot: the correlation is imprecise and shows no cause
options.why: Right: with n = 10 a correlation's confidence interval is wide, and a cross-sectional design can't show cause.

options.text: The riders were professionals, so the result can't be true
options.why: Studying pros is a limit on who it applies to, not a reason it's false.

options.text: r = 0.84 is too weak to mean anything
options.why: 0.84 is a strong correlation; the problem is the small sample and the design.

options.text: CP can't be measured after intervals
options.why: CP was measured fresh and fatigued; that is the study's method.

variants.stem: In a marathon, a runner's heart rate keeps creeping up while her pace stays the same from 25 km on. What does this most likely show?

options.text: Decoupling: internal load is rising for the same external load
options.why: Right: the heart-rate-to-pace drift Smyth used to measure durability.

options.text: Her fitness is improving during the race
options.why: Fitness doesn't change in 2 h; a rising heart rate at the same pace is a sign of drift.

options.text: Her watch is faulty, since heart rate is fixed at a given pace
options.why: Heart rate at a given pace isn't fixed in long efforts; this drift is common.

options.text: She should speed up, since her heart has spare capacity
options.why: A rising heart rate at the same pace suggests she's working closer to her limits, not further from them.

variants.stem: An Ironman triathlete sets his marathon pace from a fresh lab test of his running threshold. What is the main risk?

options.text: The pace is too fast, because the threshold has drifted after 180 km of cycling
options.why: Right: fresh zones overestimate what he can hold late in a long race.

options.text: The pace is too slow, because cycling warms up the legs
options.why: A warm-up helps short efforts; after 5 h of riding the profile has drifted down.

options.text: No risk: thresholds are fixed properties
options.why: Thresholds aren't fixed; they drift in prolonged exercise.

options.text: The pace is right, but heart rate zones will be too high
options.why: Both are off: the pace is optimistic, and heart rate at a threshold tends to rise, not fall.
